message.content:
You are an auditor on the live-spec project. Read only. Do NOT modify, create, or delete any file. Do NOT run git commands that change state. Do NOT run the pytest suite.

BACKGROUND YOU NEED
This project has a standing law, proven by its own history: **every invented ceiling goes.** On 2026-08-18 it deleted `guardrails/doc-bounds.json` and the gate that enforced it, commit `2e2f167c`, titled "Every invented ceiling goes, and the watcher that enforced them". The owner has just repeated the instruction: remove all invented thresholds and unnecessary parameters.

An invented parameter is a number, limit, cap, threshold, timeout, retry count, size bound, percentage, or magic constant that was chosen by a person or an agent rather than derived from something real. A number is NOT invented when it is a measured fact about the world (a file's install timestamp read from the filesystem, a count of things that actually exist, a version that is declared elsewhere), or when it is forced by an external contract (a protocol field width, a format the tool must emit).

The tell of an invented parameter is usually one of these: a comment justifying why the number is that number; a round number; a number a reader would have to trust rather than check; a parameter that exists so a machine can guess at something it cannot observe.

WHAT TO AUDIT
Two branches, both in this repository, both delivered today. For each, read the full diff against `origin/main`:

1. Worktree `/private/tmp/live-spec-hands/wt`, branch `fix/2026-08-19-workers-hide-work`.
   Run: `cd /private/tmp/live-spec-hands/wt && git diff origin/main...HEAD`
2. Worktree `/private/tmp/live-spec-cutm/wt`, branch `cut/2026-08-19-matrix-parts`.
   Run: `cd /private/tmp/live-spec-cutm/wt && git diff origin/main...HEAD`

The second branch is built on the first, so their diffs overlap. Report each finding once, naming which branch introduced it.

The diffs are large. Work through them systematically rather than skimming: grep the added lines for numeric literals and for words like `threshold`, `limit`, `cap`, `max`, `min`, `budget`, `timeout`, `retry`, `hours`, `seconds`, `bytes`, `count`, `size`, and read the surrounding lines of each hit.

DELIVER a list. For each candidate:
- the file and line,
- the parameter and its value,
- the exact added line or lines,
- your verdict: **invented** (chosen, not derived) or **real** (measured or externally forced), with the evidence that decided it,
- if invented: what would stand in its place if it were simply deleted — does anything break, or does the code simply stop guessing?

Also report, separately: anything else added in these two branches that looks like machinery built to service a guess rather than to check a fact. Name it and say why.

Be strict but do not manufacture findings. If a branch has no invented parameters, say so plainly. Ranking matters more than volume: put the clearest inventions first.

Answer in English. Under 80 lines.

- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

"""PreToolUse(Bash) hook: a shell never runs a command that discards uncommitted work (ROADMAP row
479, the gate's own copy in `guardrails/check-worker-restore.py`, INV-298/INV-299).

WHY THIS EVENT. `guardrails/check-worker-restore.py` catches the same five forms, but only at the
push pass's verify step — after the shell already ran the command and whatever it discarded is
already gone. Sixteen findings landed in this project's own section in one 24-hour window ending
2026-08-19 (`python3 guardrails/check-worker-restore.py --since-hours 24`: 15 ran, 1 declined), twelve
of the sixteen real discards inside live-spec's own working copies and four a fail-safe misread of a
neighbouring project's session; the worst of the twelve a worker whose brief read verbatim "HOSTILE
reviewer … Do NOT modify any file" running `git stash push -q tests/test_spec_parts.py` at
2026-08-18T07:44:14Z in `/private/tmp/live-spec-split/wt`, while a sibling agent in the same working
copy ran tests against that same file and committed it a minute later. The clause was stated in six
prose homes and caught by one retrospective gate, and workers ran the command anyway, a dozen times in
a day — a prose ban and a same-day catch are not a refusal at the moment the command is handed to a
shell. This hook is that refusal: it sits at the one point earlier than the shell itself, so the
command never runs at all rather than running and being reported afterwards.

WHAT IT CATCHES. The same five forms `check-worker-restore.py` reds on:
  - `git checkout -- <path>` and `git checkout .`, a flag standing anywhere in the command changing
    neither reading — `git checkout -q .` denies exactly as `git checkout .` does — and so does a
    treeish standing in front of a bare path with no `--` at all (`git checkout HEAD file.txt`,
    valid git that restores `file.txt` from `HEAD` and discards its uncommitted edits the same way
    `git checkout -- file.txt` does); `git checkout -b`/`-B` is branch creation, never this form, and
    is read out before either check runs, so `git checkout -b fix/x main` — a branch name and a start
    point, two bare words with no `--` — passes rather than being misread as the two-word restore
    shape above;
  - `git restore` in any form except `--staged` alone — `git restore --staged <path>` only unstages
    and leaves the working tree untouched, so it passes; adding `--worktree`/`-W` to a `--staged` call
    writes over the tree again and denies;
  - `git stash` bare, and its `push`, `save`, `create` and `store` forms — `git stash list`,
    `git stash show`, `git stash pop`, `git stash apply`, `git stash branch`, `git stash drop` and
    `git stash clear` touch no working-tree bytes belonging to the stash's target and pass;
  - `git reset` carrying `--hard`, `--merge` or `--keep`;
  - `git clean` carrying a flag with `f` or `x` in it (`-f`, `-fd`, `-fx`, `--force`, `-x`…) — UNLESS
    `-n`/`--dry-run` rides the same command, since git's own dry-run removes nothing and a flag
    ordering that would deny `git clean -fn` denies a command that deletes no file, the false refusal
    this project's own docstrings call the worse of the two failures.
A flag such as `-q` changes neither reading above; it is read past wherever it stands.

WHY NO SEAT-VERSUS-WORKER CHECK. The law forbids a WORKER this command and allows the orchestrator
(the seat's own top-level session) to run one when it owns recovery. A PreToolUse hook cannot tell
the two apart on this harness: a worker's Bash call carries the SEAT's own `transcript_path` and
`session_id`, identifiers a subagent process inherits unchanged
(`docs/prover/2026-08-17-midturn-arm-refusal.md`, the finding that retired the tool-boundary chat
arm for exactly this reason). This hook does not try. It denies the five forms for EVERY caller, seat
included, because the recovery the orchestrator needs never required one of these five commands in
the first place: reading the last committed bytes and writing them back (`git show HEAD:<path>`, then
a normal file write) reaches the same result without discarding anything a git-level command cannot
tell was uncommitted and unrelated. A hook that needed to distinguish its caller to be safe would be
the same hook that was retired six days before this one was written; this one needs no such
distinction, so the harness limit that killed the other one does not reach it.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SEE, by the same design `check-worker-restore.py` states for its own reading:
  - a heredoc BODY (`<<WORD` through its closing delimiter line) is data handed to a command, not a
    line the shell reads for commands of its own, and is dropped before segmenting;
  - a quoted span (`'…'` or `"…"`) is stepped over whole, so a forbidden form quoted inside a `grep`
    pattern or a `python3 -c "…"` script string is not read as an invocation of its own;
  - a `command`, `sudo` or `env` wrapper in front of the command is stripped, since the act belongs to
    the command it hands on (`sudo git clean -fd` discards exactly what the bare form discards); a
    wrapper carrying an option (`sudo -u x git …`) or one that takes the command as a STRING (`sh -c
    "git …"`, `xargs git …`) is out of this hook's reach, the same escape the retrospective gate
    names for the same reason.

quotes, so `cd x && git stash` and `echo done; git checkout -- .` are read as their own invocations
wherever they stand in the line.

OUTPUT SHAPE. The documented PreToolUse deny
(https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks): exit 0 with `{"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName":
"PreToolUse", "permissionDecision": "deny", "permissionDecisionReason": …}}` on stdout. The reason
names the matched form, quotes the command, and states the safe alternative in plain words: read the
old bytes with `git show HEAD:<path>` and write them back yourself — never hide the new ones.

COST. One shell command line, read once, no transcript, no state file, no network, no model call.

Repo home: hooks/worker-restore-guard.py; installed copy: ~/.claude/hooks/. Declared opt-in in
guardrails/judge-hooks.json (`library`, `opt_in_surface.worker-restore-guard: "PreToolUse"`);
installed and wired by `scripts/install-worker-restore-guard.sh`, one command, idempotent.

import re
import shlex
import sys

# file travels alone into ~/.claude/hooks/ with none of guardrails/ beside it, so importing that
# module was never an option. No test keeps the two matchers in lockstep, and they are not claimed to
# be: this hook's checkout and clean branches read a leading flag before a bare `.`, a treeish in
# front of a bare path with no `--`, and a `-n`/`--dry-run` clean call correctly, three edge cases
# classify() still reads the old, narrower way (found by adversarial review, 2026-08-19, before this
# hook first landed). check-worker-restore.py is untouched here — it is a separate, already-shipped,
# already-tested mechanism outside this delivery's brief — so the two matchers now deliberately
# disagree on those three shapes, this hook the stricter of the pair, until a session with the room to
# touch classify() and its suite closes the same gaps there.

_HEREDOC_OPENER = re.compile(r"(?<!<)<<(?!<)-?\s*(['\"]?)([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)\1")
WRAPPERS = ("command", "sudo", "env")


def _without_heredoc_bodies(command):
    lines = command.split("\n")
    kept = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(lines):
        line = lines[i]
        kept.append(line)
        i += 1
        for match in _HEREDOC_OPENER.finditer(line):
            word = match.group(2)
            while i < len(lines) and lines[i].strip() != word:
                i += 1
            if i < len(lines):
                i += 1
    return "\n".join(kept)


def _cut_on_separators(text):
    """`text` cut into segments on `&&`, `||`, `;`, `|` and newline that stand OUTSIDE quotes."""
    out = []
    buf = []
    quote = None
    i = 0
    n = len(text)
    while i < n:
        ch = text[i]
        if quote == "'":
            buf.append(ch)
            if ch == "'":
                quote = None
            i += 1
            continue
        if quote == '"':
            if ch == "\\" and i + 1 < n:
                buf.append(ch)
                buf.append(text[i + 1])
                i += 2
                continue
            buf.append(ch)
            if ch == '"':
                quote = None
            i += 1
            continue
        if ch == "\\" and i + 1 < n:
            buf.append(ch)
            buf.append(text[i + 1])
            i += 2
            continue
        if ch in "'\"":
            quote = ch
            buf.append(ch)
            i += 1
            continue
        if text[i:i + 2] in ("&&", "||"):
            out.append("".join(buf))
            buf = []
            i += 2
            continue
        if ch in (";", "|", "\n"):
            out.append("".join(buf))
            buf = []
            i += 1
            continue
        buf.append(ch)
        i += 1
    out.append("".join(buf))
    return [s.strip() for s in out if s.strip()]


def _segments(command):
    return _cut_on_separators(_without_heredoc_bodies(command))


def _tokens(segment):
    try:
        return shlex.split(segment)
    except ValueError:
        return segment.split()

    if token.startswith("-") or "=" not in token:
        return False
    head = token.split("=", 1)[0]
    return bool(head) and all(c.isalnum() or c == "_" for c in head)

    """The segment's words with leading `VAR=value` assignments and pass-through wrappers
    (`command`, `sudo`, `env`) stripped, so the first word left is the program that really runs."""
    tokens = _tokens(segment)
    while tokens:
        if _is_assignment(tokens[0]) or tokens[0].rsplit("/", 1)[-1] in WRAPPERS:
            tokens = tokens[1:]
            continue
        break
    return tokens


def _git_args(segment):
    tokens = _command_tokens(segment)
    if not tokens or tokens[0].rsplit("/", 1)[-1] != "git":
        return None
    args = tokens[1:]
    while args:
        if args[0] in ("-C", "-c", "--namespace", "--work-tree", "--git-dir") and len(args) > 1:
            args = args[2:]
        elif args[0].startswith(("--git-dir=", "--work-tree=")) \
                or (args[0].startswith("-c") and len(args[0]) > 2):
            args = args[1:]
        else:
            break
    return args


def matched_form(segment):
    """The forbidden form's name when `segment` is one of the five, else None."""
    args = _git_args(segment)
    if args is None or not args:
        return None
    sub, rest = args[0], args[1:]
    if sub == "checkout":
        if any(a in ("-b", "-B", "--orphan") for a in rest):
            pass  # branch creation: never the path-restore form, whatever else stands beside it
        else:
            non_flags = [a for a in rest if not a.startswith("-")]
            if "--" in rest or "." in non_flags or len(non_flags) >= 2:
                return "git checkout --"
    elif sub == "restore":
        if not ("--staged" in rest and "--worktree" not in rest and "-W" not in rest):
            return "git restore"
    elif sub == "stash":
        verb = next((a for a in rest if not a.startswith("-")), "")
        if verb in ("", "push", "save", "create", "store"):
            return "git stash" + (" " + verb if verb else "")
    elif sub == "reset":
        if any(a in ("--hard", "--merge", "--keep") for a in rest):
            return "git reset --hard/--merge/--keep"
    elif sub == "clean":
        is_dry_run = any(
            a == "--dry-run" or (a.startswith("-") and not a.startswith("--") and "n" in a)
            for a in rest)
        if not is_dry_run and any(a.startswith("-") and ("f" in a or "x" in a) for a in rest):
            return "git clean -f/-x"
    return None


def find_forbidden(command):
    """(segment, form) for the FIRST forbidden invocation in `command`, else (None, None)."""
    for segment in _segments(command):
        form = matched_form(segment)
        if form is not None:
            return segment, form
    return None, None


def deny_payload(segment, form):
    reason = (
        "worker-restore-guard: `%s` is a %s — it discards uncommitted work in the tree it "
        "touches, bytes a shell running this command never wrote and cannot get back (ROADMAP row "
        "479, SPEC INV-298/INV-299). Read the old bytes instead of hiding the new ones: `git show "
        "HEAD:<path>` prints the last committed content, and you write it back to the file "
        "yourself, keeping any bytes worth keeping. If the file truly needs a git-level restore, "
        "stop and say so — do not run this command." % (segment, form)
    )
    return {
        "hookSpecificOutput": {
            "hookEventName": "PreToolUse",
            "permissionDecision": "deny",
            "permissionDecisionReason": reason,
        }
    }


def main():
    raw = sys.stdin.read()
    try:
        payload = json.loads(raw) if raw.strip() else {}
    except ValueError:
        return 0
    if payload.get("tool_name") not in (None, "Bash"):
        return 0
    command = (payload.get("tool_input") or {}).get("command")
    if not isinstance(command, str) or not command.strip():
        return 0
    segment, form = find_forbidden(command)
    if segment is None:
        return 0
    print(json.dumps(deny_payload(segment, form)))
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""check-worker-restore.py — a worker never restores a working tree with a git command (row 479).

BLOCKING. A red flips the exit code to 1 and carries one parseable JSON object beside its human
lines, the gate contract's typed line (guardrails/README.md). It rebuilds no artifact and writes
nothing to disk, so the all-or-nothing write convention has nothing to hold here; it reads and
reports only.

THE LAW, in the words the five prose homes carry. Before a worker mutates a file it means to put
back, it reads that file and holds its bytes. A worker puts a file back by WRITING ITS OWN SAVED
BYTES. A worker runs no command that discards uncommitted work, in any tree: `git checkout --
<path>`, `git checkout .`, `git restore` outside `--staged`, `git stash` and its `push`, `save`,
`create` and `store` forms, `git reset` with `--hard`, `--merge` or `--keep`, and `git clean` with
`-f` or `-x`. ONE NAMED EXCEPTION (found 2026-08-19, a sandbox worker proving this very rule's own
hook): a `git clean` that also carries `-n` or `--dry-run`, bare or bundled with `-f`/`-x` in either
order (`-fn`, `-nf`, ...), removes nothing — git's own guarantee, confirmed against a real run, that
holds whichever position the flag takes and however many times `-f` also appears — so it is not
this list's finding; every other member of the list still reds exactly as it did, and a `git clean`
form this cannot prove dry still reds too. Such a command's blast radius is a PATH, so its damage
lands on files the worker never wrote and its brief never named. This rule binds a worker in every
tree, including its own isolated
worktree, since a worktree shares one repository with the lanes beside it and a worker cannot read
off its brief what else that repository holds. A worker that holds no saved bytes for a file it
mutated, or that believes a file needs a git-level restore, HALTS and reports the file and the
mutation it made, and it writes no further file and runs no further command. The orchestrator owns
recovery: it restores the named file from the last committed stage, hands the worker a fresh brief
carrying that file's current bytes, and records the halt in the row's delivery report, and the
halted work resumes under that new brief. The command list above is the one this gate reds on, word
for word — `guardrails/check-worker-restore.py`, skills/live-spec-base/SKILL.md,
skills/build-pipeline/SKILL.md, skills/build-pipeline/references/delegation-protocol.md,
templates/agent.template.md and scripts/open-lane.sh state one list, and tests/test_worker_restore.py
reds when two of them differ.

WHAT PAID FOR IT. 2026-07-23 in this repo: a caps-sweep worker ran `git checkout -- TEST_MATRIX.md`
and discarded an uncommitted format conversion, recovered only because the converter was
deterministic. 2026-07-27 in the tlvphotos tree: a worker mutated a shipped client bundle to prove a
test row red, restored it with `git checkout -- engine/assets/exhibition.js`, and three minutes
later a sibling lane began writing the sources that assemble into that same file
(inbox/2026-07-27-from-tlvphotos-worker-git-restore-discards-sibling-lanes.md). Both accounts read
as correct work, because the `git status` a careful worker pastes afterwards says "clean" in the
safe case and the destructive one alike. Prose cannot separate them; the command can.

WHAT IT OPENS. The worker-run transcripts under the harness transcript root (default
`~/.claude/projects`, overridable with `--root` or `LIVE_SPEC_TRANSCRIPT_ROOT`): every file matching
`<project-dir>/<session-id>/subagents/agent-*.jsonl`, one file per worker run. Each line is one JSON
record; the gate reads the records whose `type` is `assistant`, walks their `message.content` blocks,
and takes the `input.command` string of every block whose `type` is `tool_use` and whose `name` is
`Bash`. It reads `cwd`, `sessionId`, `agentId` and `timestamp` off the same record to name the run.

WHOSE SESSIONS IT JUDGES. The transcript root holds every session this machine ever ran, the owner's
other projects among them, and a discarding command run in another project's session is that
project's defect and not this one's — row 598 says so in its own words: "the incident belongs to
tlvphotos — its own session owns recovery and any repair — and live-spec holds the record alone".
Until 2026-08-18 the gate red on all of them alike, so a neighbour's command refused this package's
own deliveries. The gate now REDS on this project's own sessions and carries a neighbour's finding as
a notice. The key is the session's own recorded directory, the `cwd` the harness writes on every
record, checked first and alone: `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` run beside it answers a shared git
directory, and a session is a NEIGHBOUR's when that directory exists on disk right now and the answer
is a different repository from this file's own. Every worktree of this repository answers this
repository's one shared git directory, so a lane worktree is this project's session wherever on disk
it sits. The reading is fail-safe in the two cases a reader would ask about: a session whose directory
is gone by scan time (a throwaway tree, a removed worktree) and a session git cannot place are both
read as THIS project's and still red, because a gate that fell silent on what it could not place would
lose the catch it exists for.

The `cwd` is a session-wide field, though, and a session can run more than one command from more than
one directory once a `cd` moves it — a worker whose recorded `cwd` sits nowhere any repository claims
(an owner's home directory, say, the launch point rather than a checkout) can still `cd` into a real
neighbouring project and run a forbidden command there. Since 2026-08-19 that case gets one further
look, and ONLY that case: when the key itself answers nothing (`cwd` unplaceable), the gate also asks
where the one command actually ran — `effective_dir`, the directory `classify` already walks any `cd`
to and already prints as `ran in` — and if THAT directory exists on disk and git places it in a
different, nameable repository, the command is that neighbour's, not this project's, on the same
fail-safe terms as the `cwd` check above. A `cwd` the key CAN place is never second-guessed this way,
and an `effective_dir` that is itself UNKNOWN, gone from disk, unplaceable, or that lands back in this
project's own repository (a sibling worktree among them) leaves the fail-safe default exactly where it
stood before: still THIS project's, still red. A neighbour's finding is never dropped — it prints
under its own heading with session, directory, command and outcome, so the notice this package sent
tlvphotos on 2026-08-12 is still a notice a reader can write from this output. It reds nothing.

WHAT THE SHELL ANSWERED. Every `tool_use` block carries an `id`, and the shell's answer to that call
sits in the same file: a later record holding a `tool_result` block whose `tool_use_id` repeats it. A
call the harness REFUSED is marked on that answering record by a `toolDenialKind` key —
`automode-blocked`, `permission-rule`, `user-rejected` or `interrupted` — and the block carries
`is_error` true with the refusal notice as its text. Nothing reached a shell. A call that RAN carries
no such key whatever its exit status: a success comes back with the shell's stdout, and a command
that exited 1 comes back as an error carrying the shell's own complaint. Across the 2,200 worker runs
on this machine every refusal carries the key and no ordinary answer does, so the key is the whole
signal and the refusal's own text is never read for meaning. A call whose id finds no answering block
— a run cut off mid-call, a transcript still being written — has an UNKNOWN outcome. The answers are
read only from a run that already produced a finding, so a clean run costs the one pass it always
did.

WHAT A FINDING SAYS ABOUT ITS OUTCOME. Every finding names one of the three: the command RAN, the
harness DECLINED it, or the transcript gives no answer and the outcome is UNKNOWN. All three red. The
rule forbids handing such a command to a shell at all, and whether the shell obeyed lies outside the
worker's reach — the same brief and the same momentum land the destructive case on a machine whose
permissions are set one notch looser. What the outcome changes is the RECOVERY, so the findings print
ranked by the work they leave a reader: the executed ones first, then the ones with no recorded
answer, then the declined attempts. Unknown sits second because it cannot be ruled out, and a reader

+++ b/tests/test_worker_restore_guard.py
@@ -0,0 +1,282 @@
+# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
+"""tests/test_worker_restore_guard.py — hooks/worker-restore-guard.py denies the five discarding
+forms (ROADMAP row 479) AT THE SHELL BOUNDARY, before a Bash call ever runs, and denies none of the
+forms the law explicitly allows.
+
+Sixteen findings landed in this project's own section of one 24-hour window ending 2026-08-19
+(`python3 guardrails/check-worker-restore.py --since-hours 24`: 15 ran, 1 declined), twelve of them
+real discards inside this project's own working copies, caught only afterward by that retrospective
+gate. This hook is the earlier refusal; this suite proves it fires on every catch the retrospective
+gate makes and stays silent on every form the law allows — a false refusal here would stop honest
+work, which the retrospective gate's own docstring already names as the worse of the two failures.
+
+An adversarial review of this file's first landing (2026-08-19, before the fixes below) found three
+real gaps by running the shipped matcher against real git in a scratch repo: `git clean -fn` (a
+harmless dry run) was wrongly denied, and `git checkout -q .` and `git checkout HEAD file.txt` (both
+genuine discards) were wrongly passed. The cases below that name "the review" prove those three fixed
+and stay red against the pre-fix matcher.
+
+Every case runs the ACTUAL script as a subprocess against stdin JSON, the same way
+tests/test_scissors_scan.py and the other hook-red-fixtures runs already in this suite do — no
+reimplementation of the matcher is exercised here, only the shipped one.
+"""
+import json
+import os
+import subprocess
+import sys
+
+ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
+SCRIPT = os.path.join(ROOT, "hooks", "worker-restore-guard.py")
+
+
+def _run(command, tool_name="Bash"):
+    payload = {"tool_name": tool_name, "tool_input": {"command": command}, "cwd": ROOT}
+    return subprocess.run([sys.executable, SCRIPT], input=json.dumps(payload),
+                           capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=10)
+
+
+def _denied(command):
+    r = _run(command)
+    assert r.returncode == 0, r.stderr
+    assert r.stdout.strip(), "expected a deny for %r, hook was silent" % command
+    decision = json.loads(r.stdout)
+    out = decision["hookSpecificOutput"]

+#!/bin/sh
+# One-shot installer: wires hooks/worker-restore-guard.py as a PreToolUse(Bash) hook that DENIES the
+# five commands that discard uncommitted work (ROADMAP row 479, guardrails/check-worker-restore.py)
+# before the shell ever runs one — the earlier refusal the retrospective gate cannot give, since it
+# only reads a worker run's transcript afterward. Built after twelve real occurrences inside this
+# project's own working copies landed in one 24-hour window ending 2026-08-19, all past the prose ban
+# stated in six skill/template homes and past the retrospective gate that catches the same thing a day
+# late.
+#
+# Idempotent, same shape as scripts/install-separator-fence.sh: copies the file if it differs, wires
+# one PreToolUse(Bash) entry into ~/.claude/settings.json if the filename is not already present in
+# ANY existing entry's command (so a host that already wired this hook by hand, or wrapped it in a
+# personal counter, is left exactly as it stands), and self-tests before reporting success.
+#
+# Run BY THE HUMAN, once:  sh ~/live-spec/scripts/install-worker-restore-guard.sh
+# (the harness classifier blocks an agent's own hand in its configuration, deliberately — the same
+# reason scripts/install-session-hooks.sh gives for why it too must be run by a human.)
+set -e
+ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)"
+SRC="$ROOT/hooks/worker-restore-guard.py"
+DEST_DIR="$HOME/.claude/hooks"
+DEST="$DEST_DIR/worker-restore-guard.py"
+SETTINGS="$HOME/.claude/settings.json"
+
+mkdir -p "$DEST_DIR"
+
+if [ -f "$DEST" ] && cmp -s "$SRC" "$DEST"; then
+  echo "already present: $DEST"
+else
+  cp "$SRC" "$DEST"
+  chmod +x "$DEST"
+  echo "installed: $DEST"
+fi
+
+python3 - "$SETTINGS" <<'PY'
+import json, os, sys
+
+settings_path = sys.argv[1]
+cmd = "python3 ~/.claude/hooks/worker-restore-guard.py"
+fname = "worker-restore-guard.py"
+
+s = json.load(open(settings_path)) if os.path.isfile(settings_path) else {}
+pre = s.setdefault("hooks", {}).setdefault("PreToolUse", [])
+have = [h.get("command", "") for entry in pre for h in entry.get("hooks", [])]
+if any(fname in c for c in have):
+    print("already wired: PreToolUse hook %s" % fname)
+else:
+    pre.append({"matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": cmd}]})
+    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(settings_path), exist_ok=True)
+    with open(settings_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
+        json.dump(s, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
+        f.write("\n")
+    print("wired: PreToolUse hook %s -> %s" % (fname, settings_path))
+PY
+
+# Self-tests: deny on a forbidden form (plain and second-position through &&), silent on a form the
+# law allows, silent on a quoted mention.
+deny1=$(printf '%s' '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"git stash push -q tests/x.py"}}' \
+        | python3 "$DEST")
+deny2=$(printf '%s' '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"echo hi && git checkout -- ."}}' \
+        | python3 "$DEST")
+quiet1=$(printf '%s' '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"git checkout main"}}' \
+         | python3 "$DEST")
+quiet2=$(printf '%s' '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"git restore --staged x.py"}}' \
+         | python3 "$DEST")
+quiet3=$(printf '%s' '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"git stash list"}}' \
+         | python3 "$DEST")
+quiet4=$(printf '%s' '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"echo \"git stash\""}}' \
+         | python3 "$DEST")
+
+case "$deny1" in *deny*) : ;; *) echo "self-test FAILED: git stash push not denied"; exit 1;; esac
+case "$deny2" in *deny*) : ;; *) echo "self-test FAILED: second-position git checkout -- not denied"; exit 1;; esac
+[ -z "$quiet1" ] || { echo "self-test FAILED: git checkout <branch> wrongly denied"; exit 1; }
+[ -z "$quiet2" ] || { echo "self-test FAILED: git restore --staged wrongly denied"; exit 1; }

+# five commands that discard uncommitted work (ROADMAP row 479, guardrails/check-worker-restore.py)
+# before the shell ever runs one — the earlier refusal the retrospective gate cannot give, since it
+# only reads a worker run's transcript afterward. Built after twelve real occurrences inside this
+# project's own working copies landed in one 24-hour window ending 2026-08-19, all past the prose ban
+# stated in six skill/template homes and past the retrospective gate that catches the same thing a day
+# late.
+#
+# Idempotent, same shape as scripts/install-separator-fence.sh: copies the file if it differs, wires
+# one PreToolUse(Bash) entry into ~/.claude/settings.json if the filename is not already present in
+# ANY existing entry's command (so a host that already wired this hook by hand, or wrapped it in a
+# personal counter, is left exactly as it stands), and self-tests before reporting success.
+#
+# Run BY THE HUMAN, once:  sh ~/live-spec/scripts/install-worker-restore-guard.sh
+# (the harness classifier blocks an agent's own hand in its configuration, deliberately — the same
+# reason scripts/install-session-hooks.sh gives for why it too must be run by a human.)

+SRC="$ROOT/hooks/worker-restore-guard.py"

+DEST="$DEST_DIR/worker-restore-guard.py"

+import json, os, sys

+settings_path = sys.argv[1]
+cmd = "python3 ~/.claude/hooks/worker-restore-guard.py"
+fname = "worker-restore-guard.py"
+

The file carries no declared ceiling to justify it by — gate z and `guardrails/doc-bounds.json` were removed 2026-08-18 as "every invented ceiling goes" (commit `2e2f167c`), so this wish owes no urgency and no gate forces it; it is asked for readability and edit cost alone, the same reason the spec was split, and a session picking this up should not invent itself a deadline the tree no longer states. PRODUCT_SPEC.md was already cut this way: a 50-kilobyte core plus thirty `spec/*.md` parts, joined back by `guardrails/specformat.py`'s `spec_paths`/`read_document`, one committed `PRODUCT_SPEC.index.md` standing in for the code-to-location table the core no longer embeds, and one reader node in `tests/conftest.py` so every caller still sees one document whether it is one file or thirty. The investigation checked four claimed risks against the matrix rather than trusting them, and found three real in some degree and one flatly wrong: (1) *true* — `scripts/build-matrix-reference.py` and `guardrails/check-matrix-reference.py` each read exactly one file; the spec's sibling scripts already read a core-plus-parts list through `specformat.spec_paths`/`read_document`, so the plumbing exists already and the matrix needs wiring rather than invention. (2) *overstated* — of 62 test files naming TEST_MATRIX.md, 44 already route through `tests/conftest.py`'s shared `read()`/`read_flat()`; only nine still open the file by path directly and need converting: `test_class_hunt.py`, `test_config_health.py`, `test_cross_surface_policy.py`, `test_gesture_overlay_parity.py`, `test_founding_set_version.py`, `test_impact_analysis_entry.py`, `test_paired_transition.py`, `test_prose_gate.py`, `test_scenario_entry_exit.py`. (3) *false as a blocker* — the INV-xxx anchors a matrix row trails are plain text read per row wherever that row physically sits; a file split does not touch them. (4) *false* — no byte ceiling governs either TEST_MATRIX.md or ARCHITECTURE.md today, so there is no size-based reason to prefer one over the other. *The block risk that turned the stop*: the matrix's `## Reference` is documented (`docs/test-matrix-format.md`) as *embedded* in the body, and `specformat.read_document` concatenates a named core's own full text before any of its parts — so a Reference left embedded in a shrunk core would sit ahead of every part, and the twenty-three node blocks appended after it would land after the Reference too, breaking the parser that expects the Reference last. The spec hit this identical shape and solved it by moving its Reference out to its own committed file (`PRODUCT_SPEC.index.md`) and re-synthesizing it at read time, appended after the whole concatenation (`tests/conftest.py`'s `_with_reference_tail`); the matrix needs that same move, and making it is a change to `docs/test-matrix-format.md`'s own documented shape, which is itself subject to the format family's comprehension gate — mechanical lints, then a panel of cold readers, passing only after two consecutive reads return zero blocking findings — a review loop one agent's single pass does not honestly close alone. Not done by: shrinking the file without the reader node, leaving the Reference embedded in the core, or skipping the cold reads because the ceiling that used to force this work is gone |
1521:+## Parts map
1908:+2. **The Parts map** — a table naming every part file the matrix's rows live in, one row per part. Its order is the order a reader should read the parts in. A part is a file under `matrix/`, holding one architecture node's whole block of rows. The map names each part's row count and its topic line, the node's own responsibility line carried over from `ARCHITECTURE.md`. Together they let a reader judge a part's size and purpose before opening it.
1912:+A reader who wants the whole matrix as one document reads it through the shared reader rather than opening TEST_MATRIX.md alone. `guardrails/specformat.py`'s `spec_paths()` and `read_document()` join the core and the parts the Parts map names into one body, in map order. This is the same join the spec's own core and parts already use. A gate or a builder script takes the core, then each part, on its command line, and reads them this way. The test suite goes one step further. `tests/conftest.py`'s `read()` takes that joined body and appends the committed `TEST_MATRIX.index.md` under a synthesized `## Reference` heading. A test that calls `read("TEST_MATRIX.md")` then sees the core, every part, and the Reference, exactly as if the file had never been split.
1930:+The spec groups its criteria into named cases. The matrix groups its rows into node blocks: one block per architecture node, headed `### [node: <name>]`, and the block heading is the matrix's case grouping. Each node block is its own file under `matrix/`, named after the node. Any `[target]` marker is dropped from the filename only, never from the heading text. A node the architecture marks `[target]` — promised under an owned queue row, its machinery not yet landed — keeps that mark in its block heading, so the matrix and the architecture read the same. Every architecture node owns at least one block, and every module block owns at least one row that asserts the module at its declared interface. A new row is written into its node's own part file under `matrix/`, the file the Parts map names for that node, never into TEST_MATRIX.md.
